walkthrough:
Read Start and End Values Carefully**
You are sitting with Fig. 5.1. In 1998 the white bar for daisies is about 50% and the grey bar for normal poppy is also about 50%. The black bar for biotype X is barely visible at about 1%. By 2003 the white is about 15%, the grey is about 15%, and the black is about 70%. Always quote % frequency and allow small reading error.

Describe Each Group Separately Then Together**
Daisies and normal poppies both show a decrease over the six years. Biotype X shows the opposite - a large increase. If you add grey + black, total poppies go from about 52% to about 85%, so poppies as a whole increase while daisies decrease.

Add Pattern Detail for Extra Marks**
Two useful extra observations are that daisies and normal poppies stay equal in every year, and that change is slow from 1998 to 2001 then very steep from 2001 to 2003. That steep phase is when biotype X jumps from about 10% to 40% to 70%.

Final answer: Daisies and normal red poppies decreased overall from approx. 50% to 15% between 1998 and 2003. Biotype X red poppy increased from approx. 1% to 70%. Total poppies increased from approx. 52% to 85%. Daisies and normal poppies remained equal to each other throughout, with the most rapid change after 2001.

hints: Think about what a change from proline to leucine at position 197 really means for the protein chain itself.
Recall how the order of amino acids controls the way the whole enzyme folds into its 3D shape.
Link that change in 3D shape to what can or cannot fit into the enzyme, and whether the enzyme can still do its normal job.
walkthrough:
From Gene to Primary Structure**
The mutation is in the gene coding for acetolactate synthetase. That changes one codon, so one amino acid in the polypeptide swaps from proline to leucine. That is by definition a change in primary structure.

From Primary to Tertiary and Active Site**
Different amino acids have different sizes, charges and bonding properties. Proline is very rigid and kinks chains, leucine is different. So hydrogen, ionic and hydrophobic bonds reform in new places and the enzyme folds differently. That means a change in tertiary or 3D globular structure, especially around the binding site.

Effect on Inhibitor Versus Substrate**
Metsulfuron-methyl normally fits into the enzyme and blocks it. After the shape change, the herbicide no longer fits well enough to inhibit, but the active site still accepts the normal substrate to form an enzyme-substrate complex. So the enzyme still functions to make the three essential amino acids for growth.

Final answer: Change in primary structure leads to change in tertiary / 3D structure of acetolactate synthetase. Shape of active site is altered so metsulfuron-methyl can no longer bind / inhibit it, but the enzyme can still bind substrate and synthesise essential amino acids.

hints: Consider what the altered enzyme means for biotype X when the field is sprayed with metsulfuron-methyl: does it die like normal poppies, or can it survive and keep growing?
walkthrough:
Relate Enzyme Function to Plant Survival**
Metsulfuron-methyl kills weeds by blocking amino acid synthesis. Because biotype X has a modified enzyme that is not inhibited, it continues to make essential amino acids even when sprayed. Therefore, the poppies are resistant, survive the herbicide treatment, and continue to grow.
Final answer: Biotype X red poppies are resistant to metsulfuron-methyl / survive / are not killed / continue growing in its presence.

hints: Compare total weeds in 2003 with 1998 using Fig. 5.1 - what has happened to the black bar and what does that mean for herbicide control?
Think about which weed type now dominates and whether the spray will still kill it.
Link more surviving weeds to what happens to wheat plants growing in the same field for light, water, space and mineral ions.
walkthrough:
Predict the Weed to Wheat Ratio**
In 1998 almost all weeds were sensitive and controlled, with biotype X at only about 1%. By 2003 biotype X is about 70% and total weeds are high. So the herbicide is largely failing and there will be more weeds and proportionally less wheat than in 1998.

Explain Why Control Fails**
The dominant weed is now biotype X. Its altered acetolactate synthetase is not inhibited, so it survives spraying, grows, flowers and sets seed. Daisies and normal poppies are still killed, but they are now only about 15% each.

Link to Competition**
More surviving poppies means wheat seedlings compete more intensely for the same limited resources - light for photosynthesis, space for leaves and roots, water and mineral ions such as nitrate and magnesium from soil. That reduces wheat growth and yield relative to weeds.

Final answer: In 2003 compared to 1998 there is a higher proportion of weeds to wheat / more weeds and less wheat. Most weeds are now biotype X which is resistant to / not killed by metsulfuron-methyl. Wheat faces more competition for light, space, water and mineral ions.

hints: Think about what metsulfuron-methyl was doing as a selective agent - what happens to that selective force when you stop using it?
Consider whether the leucine version of the enzyme gives any advantage when the old herbicide is gone and a different enzyme is now attacked.
Follow through to survival, reproduction and allele frequency of biotype X, and whether evolution could start again against the new spray.
walkthrough:
Selection Pressure Is Removed**
Continuous metsulfuron-methyl gave biotype X a huge advantage - sensitive plants died, resistant plants survived. Stop that herbicide and that specific advantage disappears. There is now a new selection pressure from the different herbicide.

Resistance Allele Becomes Useless**
The proline to leucine change only protects acetolactate synthetase. It gives no protection against a herbicide that inhibits a different target enzyme. So biotype X is now just as sensitive as other weeds to the new spray, will die or fail to breed, and will pass on its allele less often.

Abundance Falls But Evolution Can Repeat**
As a result, numbers and frequency of biotype X fall over generations. However, mutation is random and ongoing, so a different mutation affecting the new target enzyme could arise and be selected for, starting resistance evolution again.

Final answer: Selection pressure from metsulfuron-methyl is removed / changed. The resistance allele is no longer advantageous / selected for, so biotype X plants are killed by the new herbicide / do not survive to breed and their abundance decreases. A new mutation could in time give resistance to the new herbicide.
